title: Seven Loaves, Half-Sight, and the Road of the Cross
summary: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves, refuses the Pharisees' demand for a sign, and rebukes his disciples for failing to understand the bread. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. Near Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, die, and rise, and that anyone who follows him must take up a cross.
story:
This is the hinge of Mark's Gospel. For eight chapters the question has been who Jesus is, asked by crowds (1:27), opponents (2:7), disciples in a storm (4:41), his hometown (6:2-3), and a frightened king (6:14-16). Here Peter gives the right answer, and at once Jesus redefines it: the Christ must suffer. From this point the story turns toward Jerusalem. Each of the three predictions of the passion (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34) is followed by the disciples' misunderstanding and by Jesus' teaching on what following him costs.

The chapter also closes the bread section that began in chapter 6. The second feeding, set in the largely Gentile country east of the lake, echoes the first; the Pharisees' demand for a sign shows that more wonders will not produce faith; the argument about one loaf in the boat shows that even the disciples have not understood what they saw; and the blind man who sees only partly at first sets the pattern for Peter at Caesarea Philippi, who sees the right title but not its meaning. The two halves meet in one theme: the disciples have eyes and do not yet see, and the sight they need will come only by way of the cross.
historical:
The place names in the chapter follow Jesus around the edges of Galilee. Dalmanutha (verse 10) is known from no other ancient source; Matthew's parallel has Magadan (Matthew 15:39), also otherwise unknown, and many later manuscripts of both Gospels change the name to Magdala, the fishing town on the lake's western shore. Bethsaida (verse 22) lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee from the north, in the territory of Herod Philip. Josephus says Philip raised the village to the rank of a city and named it Julias after the emperor Augustus' daughter (Antiquities 18.28), which may be why Mark still calls it a village (verses 23 and 26). Its site is disputed between et-Tell, excavated since 1987 under Rami Arav, and el-Araj nearer the shore, excavated since 2016 under Mordechai Aviam and R. Steven Notley.

Caesarea Philippi lay about forty kilometers (twenty-five miles) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, beside the spring at Banias that is one of the sources of the Jordan. A cave there held a shrine to the Greek god Pan, which gave the place its older name, Paneas. Josephus says Herod the Great built a temple of white marble there in honor of Augustus (Jewish War 1.404-406; Antiquities 15.363-364), and that his son Philip enlarged the town and named it Caesarea, for the emperor, with his own name added to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast (Antiquities 18.28; Jewish War 2.168). Where Herod's temple stood is debated: Ehud Netzer and Zvi Uri Maoz proposed structures at Banias itself, while Andrew Overman, excavating since 1999 at Omrit, a few kilometers to the southwest, argued that the temple there is Herod's Augusteum. Either way, the region was thoroughly Gentile, marked by pagan worship and imperial loyalty. Mark says the conversation took place ‘on the way’ to the villages around it (verse 27), away from Jewish crowds and in sight of Rome's claims.

A demand for a ‘sign from heaven’ (verse 11) had a particular meaning in first-century Judea. Josephus tells of popular prophets who promised signs to their followers: Theudas, under the governor Fadus (around AD 44 to 46), led a crowd to the Jordan, claiming he would divide the river (Antiquities 20.97-98), and an Egyptian prophet under Felix promised that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.169-172; compare Acts 21:38). Josephus says such men led people into the wilderness promising that God would show them signs of freedom (Jewish War 2.259). These episodes come after Jesus' ministry, but they show what a sign meant to many: a public wonder that would authenticate a leader and begin Israel's liberation.

Messianic hope took several forms. The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, describe a coming son of David, the Lord's anointed, who would drive the Gentiles from Jerusalem, purge the city, and gather a holy people (Psalm of Solomon 17). The Community Rule from Qumran speaks of the coming of a prophet and of messiahs of Aaron and of Israel, a priestly and a royal figure (1QS 9:11), and another Qumran text says heaven and earth will listen to God's messiah, in a passage that also speaks of healing the wounded and raising the dead (4Q521). A victorious king was the dominant picture. No Jewish text before Jesus clearly speaks of a Messiah who would be rejected by Israel's leaders, killed, and raised. The elders, chief priests, and scribes named in verse 31 were the three groups that together made up the Jerusalem council, the Sanhedrin (compare 14:53 and 15:1).

Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, bandits, and rebels, carried out publicly as a warning. After Herod the Great's death in 4 BC, the Roman governor of Syria, Varus, crushed a revolt that had spread to Galilee and crucified about two thousand men (Antiquities 17.295; Jewish War 2.75). A condemned man was usually made to carry the crossbeam to the place of execution; Plutarch mentions in passing that each criminal who is punished carries out his own cross (On the Delays of the Divine Vengeance 9, Moralia 554B). In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail still through it. When Jesus speaks of taking up the cross, his hearers would picture that walk.
cultural:
The second feeding is set, by the flow of the story since 7:31, in or near the Decapolis. The crowd has been with Jesus for three days, some have come ‘a great distance’ (verse 3), and they have nothing left to eat, so the scene has the feel of an assembly in the wilderness like Israel's in the time of Moses. The Greek word for basket differs from the first feeding. There Mark uses kophinos, a wicker basket that Roman writers associated with Jews: the satirist Juvenal twice mocks Jews in Rome for their basket and hay (Satires 3.14 and 6.542). Here he uses spyris, a basket that could be large enough to hold a man, as when Paul was let down over the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25). The meal follows the pattern of a Jewish meal: the host takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it out (verse 6), the same four actions that will recur at the Last Supper (14:22).

Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back from one batch to raise the next. Because a small amount works through the whole, it was a ready image for influence, good or bad (in Jesus' parable in Matthew 13:33 it is good). At Passover Israel removed all leaven from the house (Exodus 12:15-20), so leaven often stood for corruption, and Paul uses it that way (1 Corinthians 5:6-8; Galatians 5:9). Luke glosses the leaven of the Pharisees as hypocrisy (Luke 12:1). The Herod of verse 15 is Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea (4 BC to AD 39), who had executed John the Baptist (6:14-29), and the Pharisees had already plotted with Herod's supporters against Jesus (3:6). What their leaven shares Mark leaves to the reader: an unbelief that demands signs and a power that silences prophets.

The rebuke scene reverses the customs of teacher and disciple. A disciple walked behind his teacher, learned from him, and did not correct him in public. Peter takes Jesus aside and ‘began to rebuke’ him (verse 32), using the verb Mark has used for Jesus silencing demons and the storm (1:25; 4:39). Jesus turns, looks at all the disciples, and rebukes Peter in their sight. His words, ‘Get behind me’, use the same phrase (opisō mou) as his first call, ‘Come, follow me’, literally ‘come behind me’ (1:17), and as verse 34, ‘If anyone wants to come after me’: Peter is sent back to the disciple's place. The name Satan means adversary; in Job 1 to 2 and Zechariah 3 the satan is the accuser, and Mark's Satan has already tested Jesus in the wilderness (1:13). Peter's words, meant as loyalty, repeat the tempter's offer of a road without suffering.

The closing sayings belong to an honor culture. In the ancient Mediterranean world a person's worth was measured by public reputation, and crucifixion was designed to strip a man of honor as well as life; Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross “scorning its shame.” To be ashamed of Jesus and his words (verse 38) was to side with public opinion against a condemned man. ‘This adulterous and sinful generation’ echoes the prophets, who called Israel's unfaithfulness to God adultery (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3), and the soul's value in verses 36 and 37 is set in the language of trade: gain, profit, loss, and what one could give in exchange.
literary:
Mark builds the chapter so that each part explains the others. Verses 1 to 21 repeat the pattern of 6:30 to 7:37: a feeding, a crossing of the lake, a dispute with Pharisees, and a scene in which the disciples fail to understand. The pattern ends with a string of seven questions from Jesus in verses 17 to 21, the sharpest in the Gospel. He asks whether their hearts are hardened, the word Mark used of the disciples in 6:52 and of the Pharisees in 3:5, and he quotes the prophets' charge against Israel, ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ (verse 18), which echoes Jeremiah 5:21, “who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear” and Ezekiel 12:2, and recalls Isaiah 6:9-10 as Jesus used it of outsiders in 4:12. The disciples now stand where the outsiders stood. The only bread they have in the boat is ‘one loaf’ (verse 14), and many readers see a hint that the one loaf they fail to notice is Jesus himself.

Immediately a blind man is healed in two stages (verses 22 to 26), the only healing in the Gospels that happens in stages. First he sees people ‘like trees walking around’, then everything clearly. The scene works as an acted parable of the disciples: at Caesarea Philippi Peter sees partly, knowing the right title but not what it means, and the second touch, clear sight, will come only through the cross. The blind man at Bethsaida and blind Bartimaeus at Jericho (10:46-52) frame the whole next section of the Gospel, 8:22 to 10:52, which Mark marks with the phrase ‘on the way’ (8:27; 9:33-34; 10:32, 52). Within that frame come the three predictions of the passion, each followed by misunderstanding and by teaching on discipleship.

Verses 27 to 33 are the center of the Gospel. Jesus asks two questions, first what people say and then what the disciples say, and Peter's answer, ‘You are the Christ’ (verse 29), takes up the title of the book's first line (1:1). Then comes the turn: ‘He began to teach them’ (verse 31), and the word ‘must’ (dei) signals divine necessity. Mark adds that Jesus said this ‘quite frankly’ (parrēsia, openly, verse 32), in contrast to the parables and hidden sayings of earlier chapters (4:33-34): the secret of his identity is now spoken plainly to the disciples, and it is the cross. The verb rebuke appears three times in quick succession, Jesus rebuking the disciples to silence (verse 30), Peter rebuking Jesus (32), and Jesus rebuking Peter (33), and the struggle it traces is over what kind of Messiah Jesus is. The chapter ends with four sayings joined by the word ‘for’ (verses 35 to 38), each giving the reason for the one before, and it plays on the double sense of psychē, life and soul: the one who clutches his life loses it, and no gain can buy back a forfeited soul.

outline.t: Four thousand fed with seven loaves
The leaven of the Pharisees and Herod; the disciples' dullness
A blind man healed in two stages
The first passion prediction and Peter's rebuke

doctrines.note: Peter's confession, ‘You are the Christ’ (verse 29), is true, and Jesus accepts it, but he immediately fills the title with new content: the Messiah is the Son of Man who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. The kingship is real, drawn from Psalm 2 and 2 Samuel 7, and the road to it runs through the cross. Mark will not let his readers separate the title from the suffering.

The passion prediction says that Jesus' death is not an accident or a tragic defeat but something that ‘must’ happen within God's purpose (verse 31). This chapter states the necessity; Mark explains its meaning in 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many, and in the words over the cup at the Last Supper (14:24). The saying that nothing can be given in exchange for a soul (verse 37) prepares for the one who gives his own life as the ransom.

The Pharisees demand a sign and will not believe; the disciples have seen signs and still do not understand. Faith in this chapter is not produced by proof on demand. It comes as sight given by Jesus himself, sometimes in stages, and it is expressed in following him on the way.

Verse 38 is the first saying in Mark about the Son of Man coming ‘in His Father's glory with the holy angels’, language drawn from Daniel 7:13-14 and Zechariah 14:5. The one who is about to be rejected and killed will come again as judge, and how people respond to him and his words now will matter then. The same promise returns before the high priest (14:62).

Following Jesus means denying oneself and taking up the cross (verse 34). The kingdom's logic reverses ordinary values: whoever loses his life for Jesus and the gospel will save it, and no gain, even the whole world, is worth the loss of one's soul. The call is addressed to the crowd as well as the disciples, so it is the normal shape of discipleship, not a special vocation for a few.

words.note: Christos, anointed one, the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, messiah. In Israel kings, priests, and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to mark them as set apart by God (1 Samuel 16:13; Leviticus 4:3), and the king was ‘the LORD's anointed’. By the first century the word had come to mean the promised king from David's line. It occurs more than 500 times in the New Testament but only seven times in Mark (1:1; 8:29; 9:41; 12:35; 13:21; 14:61; 15:32). Peter's use of it is the first time in Mark that a disciple names Jesus with the title from the book's opening line.

Dei, it is necessary, it must; about a hundred times in the New Testament, six in Mark. Here it governs the whole prediction: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. The necessity is not blind fate but the purpose of God revealed in Scripture, as Mark's ‘it is written’ in 9:12 and 14:21 makes clear. Luke especially develops the word, and the risen Jesus asks whether the Christ did not have to suffer these things (Luke 24:26).

Aparneomai, to deny, disown, or renounce; about eleven times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels. Here Jesus asks disciples to deny themselves, that is, to disown the self's claim to rule. The same verb describes Peter's denial of Jesus in 14:30, 31, and 72. Mark's readers would notice the irony: the disciple who refused to let Jesus deny himself the cross later denied his Lord, while Jesus did not spare himself but went to the cross.

Psychē, life or soul; about 103 times in the New Testament, eight in Mark. The word covers physical life and the person's inner self, the living person as a whole, as the Hebrew nephesh does, rather than a detachable part. Jesus plays on the range: whoever tries to keep his life will lose it, and no gain can buy back a forfeited soul (verses 35 to 37). English Bibles switch between life and soul in these verses, but it is the same Greek word throughout, and in 10:45 the Son of Man gives his psychē as a ransom.

Sēmeion, sign; about seventy-seven times in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it names the signs God gave through Moses in Egypt (Exodus 4:8-9) and the signs that confirm a prophet's word (Deuteronomy 13:1-2; Isaiah 7:11). A ‘sign from heaven’ (verse 11) was a public wonder that would prove God's backing on demand. Mark never calls Jesus' mighty works signs; the word appears in Mark mostly for the Pharisees' demand and for the false signs of the end (13:22). Jesus refuses to perform to order.

Pōroō, to harden, make dull or insensitive; five times in the New Testament (Mark 6:52; 8:17; John 12:40; Romans 11:7; 2 Corinthians 3:14). The related noun describes the hardness of heart Jesus grieves over in the Pharisees (3:5). In Mark it is the disciples, not only opponents, whose hearts are hardened, a frank portrait that warns readers that closeness to Jesus is not the same as understanding him.

Zymē, leaven or yeast; thirteen times in the New Testament. It means the fermented dough that raises a whole batch. Jesus uses it once as an image of the kingdom's hidden growth (Matthew 13:33), but more often, as here and in Paul (1 Corinthians 5:6-8; Galatians 5:9), as an image of a corrupting influence that spreads unseen. The disciples hear the word and think only of their empty bread supply.

Stauros, cross; about twenty-seven times in the New Testament, four in Mark (8:34; 15:21, 30, 32). In Greek it meant an upright stake and then the Roman instrument of execution. This is the first time the word appears in Mark, before any mention of how Jesus will die, and it appears in a command to the crowd. Paul calls the message of the cross foolishness to the world and the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18).

christ:
Peter's confession states who Jesus is, and Jesus' teaching states what he came to do. He is the Christ, Israel's anointed king, the son of David promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and addressed by God in Psalm 2. But he immediately speaks of himself as the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 who comes with the clouds and receives “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:14), and he says that before that glory the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise after three days. The chapter joins what Peter wanted to keep apart, the crown and the cross.

Mark does not quote a text for the ‘must’, but the vocabulary points to the Scriptures Jesus will cite later. The verb for being rejected (apodokimazō) is the verb of Psalm 118:22 in the Greek Old Testament, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” which Jesus quotes of himself in 12:10. The servant of Isaiah 53 is “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3), and in 10:45 the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many, language widely read as an echo of that chapter. Rising ‘after three days’ may recall Hosea 6:2, “on the third day He will raise us up,” where Israel's restoration is pictured as resurrection. These links are allusions rather than formal quotations, but together they show a Messiah who fulfills Israel's story by suffering on its behalf.

The chapter also shows the Messiah's character. He has compassion on a hungry crowd that includes Gentiles (verse 2), the same word Mark used of the first feeding (6:34). He sighs deeply at the demand for a sign (verse 12), refusing to prove himself on others' terms, as he refused Satan in the wilderness. He is patient with disciples who still see people like trees walking, and he gives sight in two touches. The one who gives sight in stages will open his disciples' eyes the same way, through the cross and the empty tomb. Finally, verse 38 shows that the Son of Man who is about to be shamed will come in his Father's glory with the holy angels as judge, so that the one condemned by the elders, chief priests, and scribes is the one before whom all will stand. The confession of the church, that the crucified Jesus is Lord and will come again, is already present in seed in this chapter.
interpretation:
Jewish interpretation has long seen the Messiah as the one who brings Israel's redemption and victory, which is why the idea of a crucified Messiah was, as Paul put it, “a stumbling block to Jews” (1 Corinthians 1:23). Some later Jewish traditions do speak of a suffering or slain messianic figure. The Targum of Jonathan on the Prophets, an Aramaic paraphrase read in the synagogue, renders Isaiah 52:13 as ‘my servant the Messiah’ but applies the passage's sufferings to Israel and the nations rather than to him. The Babylonian Talmud tells of a Messiah son of Joseph who will be slain, reading Zechariah 12:10 of him (Sukkah 52a). Medieval commentators such as Rashi read the servant of Isaiah 53 as the people of Israel suffering among the nations, and Origen reports already in the third century that a Jewish scholar he debated read the passage that way (Against Celsus 1.55). Jewish readers of Mark therefore rightly press the question the chapter raises: whether a rejected and executed man can be the Messiah at all.

In the early church the confession was read mostly through Matthew's longer version with its saying about the rock and the keys (Matthew 16:16-19). Origen (Commentary on Matthew 12.10-11) taught that every disciple who confesses Christ as Peter did becomes a rock, while later Roman bishops read the rock as Peter and his successors, and Augustine in his Retractations admitted he had held both that the rock was Peter and that it was Christ confessed. Mark's shorter version, without the blessing of Peter but with the rebuke, drew less attention. Augustine's Sermon 96 (numbered 46 in some older English collections) expounds Mark 8:34, arguing that the command to deny oneself is not grievous because the one who commands helps his hearers to obey, and that a person lost by loving himself is found by denying himself. In the fifteenth century Thomas à Kempis gave the command its most famous devotional treatment in The Imitation of Christ, whose chapter on ‘the royal way of the holy cross’ (book 2, chapter 12) begins from this saying. Ignatius of Loyola, by Jesuit tradition, repeated verse 36 to his roommate Francis Xavier at the University of Paris in the early 1530s until Xavier gave up his academic ambitions, and the verse appears often in Xavier's later letters.

The Reformers read Peter's rebuke as the temptation of every theology that wants glory without suffering. Martin Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518, theses 19 to 21) contrasted the theologian of glory, who looks for God in visible power and success, with the theologian of the cross, who finds God in suffering and weakness, and his contrast has been read ever since as a commentary on Caesarea Philippi. John Calvin devoted two chapters of the Institutes (3.7 and 3.8) to self-denial and bearing the cross as the pattern of the Christian life. In the twentieth century Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Nachfolge (1937; in English The Cost of Discipleship, 1948), written as the church in Germany faced the Nazi state, set against cheap grace a grace that calls a person to follow Jesus to the cross, and his own execution in 1945 gave the book its weight.

Modern critical study made verse 31 a test case. William Wrede (1901) read the passion predictions as part of Mark's theology of the messianic secret, and Rudolf Bultmann (History of the Synoptic Tradition, 1921) treated them as prophecies composed after the event. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) argued, on the contrary, that Jesus expected the end to come soon and went to Jerusalem to die in order to force its arrival. Hans F. Bayer (Jesus' Predictions of Vindication and Resurrection, 1986) and N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) argued that Jesus did foresee and interpret his death, and Robert Fowler (Loaves and Fishes, 1981) studied the two feedings as a pair built by Mark for his readers. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Mark 8:31-38 is read on the Second Sunday in Lent in Year B and Mark 8:27-38 on Proper 19; the Roman lectionary reads 8:27-35 on the Twenty-Fourth Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year B. Charles William Everest's hymn ‘Take Up Thy Cross, the Savior Said’ (1833), one of the few American hymns taken into the English Hymns Ancient and Modern (1861), versifies verse 34.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

Verse 1: most early manuscripts read ‘again a large crowd’, while the Byzantine text, followed by the King James Version, reads ‘a very great multitude’, from a similar-looking Greek word. Verse 10: the name Dalmanutha puzzled copyists, and some manuscripts substitute Magdala, Magada, or other forms; the BSB follows the oldest witnesses.

Verse 15: some early manuscripts, including the Chester Beatty papyrus P45 and Codex Washingtonianus, read ‘the leaven of the Herodians’, matching 3:6 and 12:13, where most read ‘the leaven of Herod’. Matthew has ‘the Pharisees and Sadducees’ (Matthew 16:6), and Luke 12:1 ‘the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy’.

Verse 26: many later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, expand the ending to ‘Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town’. The shorter text is found in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and the additions look like attempts to make it match the other commands to silence.

Verse 31: Mark says the Son of Man will rise ‘after three days’, while Matthew and Luke say ‘on the third day’ (Matthew 16:21; Luke 9:22), the phrase of the early creed in 1 Corinthians 15:4. The two expressions were used interchangeably in Jewish reckoning, where part of a day counted as a day. Verse 34: some manuscripts read elthein, ‘to come’ after me, and others akolouthein, ‘to follow’; the Nestle-Aland edition prints the second and the SBL edition the first, with no difference in sense. Verse 38: a few witnesses, including P45 and Codex Washingtonianus, lack the word ‘words’, giving ‘whoever is ashamed of me and of mine’, meaning Jesus' followers; the longer text is far better attested.

Translation also matters in verses 35 to 37, where the same Greek word, psychē, is rendered ‘life’ in verse 35 and ‘soul’ in verses 36 and 37 in the BSB, ESV, and KJV, while the NRSV and NIV use ‘life’ throughout. Either choice captures part of the word; the saying depends on hearing both.

teach.big: Jesus is the Christ, but the Christ he is must suffer, die, and rise, and following him means walking the same road of the cross, the only road on which our eyes are fully opened and our lives are truly saved.

outline.t: Jesus' compassion reaches a hungry crowd at the edge of Israel, and what the disciples cannot supply he multiplies from what they have.
Demanding that God prove himself on our terms is not faith; Jesus refuses to perform, and he grieves over the heart that asks.
Even disciples can have eyes that do not see; Jesus answers our anxious small thinking by asking us to remember what he has already done.
Jesus sometimes gives sight in stages, and partial sight is a step, not the goal; he keeps touching until we see clearly.
Everyone must finally answer Jesus' own question, and the right answer is that he is the Christ, though the title still has to be learned.
A Messiah without a cross is a human idea, even a satanic one; God's way to glory runs through rejection, death, and resurrection.
The cross is the shape of every disciple's life: losing ourselves for Jesus and the gospel is how our lives are saved, and nothing we could gain is worth our souls.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading uses verse 34 to describe any hardship as ‘my cross to bear’: an illness, a difficult relative, bad luck. In Mark the cross is the cost of following Jesus, the suffering that comes from loyalty to him and the gospel, and the self-denial chosen for his sake. Ordinary suffering can be carried in faith, but flattening the word empties Jesus' call of its sharpness. A second pitfall is to preach self-denial as self-hatred or the erasure of personality. Jesus calls disciples to renounce the self's rule, not the self God made, and he promises that those who lose their lives for his sake will save them.

A third error turns Peter into a fool, when Peter's rebuke is the natural reaction of anyone who loves Jesus and shares the common hope. The point is that sincere devotion can still oppose God's way, and Jesus looks at all the disciples as he rebukes him. A fourth draws allegories from every detail of the feedings (the seven loaves, the four thousand) that the text does not support; Jesus himself directs attention only to the leftovers and the numbers of baskets (verses 19 and 20), and interpreters should hold symbolic readings lightly. A fifth reads the two-stage healing as proof that Jesus' power was limited or that healing ministries should expect partial results; Mark tells it as an acted parable of the disciples' gradual sight. Finally, avoid preaching verse 36 as a general warning against materialism alone. It warns against every gain, including religious reputation and security, that is bought by refusing Jesus' road.
teach.pastoral: Verse 34 is often misused against people who are being harmed. Victims of abuse or domestic violence have been told that submitting to mistreatment is their cross. The text does not say so: the cross in Mark is taken up for Jesus and the gospel, not imposed by an abuser, and Jesus' own teaching elsewhere protects the little ones (9:42). Teach it so that no one in the room hears a command to stay in danger. The chapter also speaks to people who feel their faith is only partial or their understanding slow; the blind man seeing trees walking and the disciples' repeated failures show that Jesus does not abandon those who see only in part. Those who suffer for their faith, in hostile workplaces or families or under governments that persecute Christians, will hear verses 35 to 38 as both comfort and summons, and teachers should honor that weight without romanticizing suffering.

hard.q: Is the feeding of the four thousand a second event, or a retelling of the feeding of the five thousand?
hard.a:
The objection rests on how alike the two stories are: a crowd in a desolate place, disciples who do not know where bread will come from, Jesus taking, giving thanks, breaking, and giving, everyone satisfied, and baskets of leftovers. Form critics following Rudolf Bultmann concluded that Mark received two versions of one tradition, perhaps told in different communities, and included both, and many critical scholars still hold that view. The strongest form of the objection is the disciples' question in verse 4. If they had seen Jesus feed five thousand only weeks before, their asking where bread could be found looks less like forgetfulness than like a sign that the story was first told on its own. Skeptical readers take the doublet as evidence that Mark assembled his Gospel from traditions without regard to historical sequence.

Others answer that the details differ consistently: five loaves and seven, two fish and a few small fish, five thousand and four thousand, twelve baskets and seven, a different word for basket, a Jewish setting and an apparently Gentile one, one day and three days. Commentators who read them as two events, such as R. T. France, note that Jesus himself refers to both feedings as separate events in verses 19 and 20, that Matthew also includes both (Matthew 14:13-21; 15:32-39), and that repeating a sign in a different place with a different crowd is the kind of thing a teacher might well do. They add that the disciples' failure to expect a second miracle is exactly Mark's point, made explicit in verses 17 to 21, and fits their earlier failure after the first feeding (6:52). Scholars who study Mark as a narrative, like Robert Fowler (1981), argue that on either historical view Mark means the two feedings to be read together. Readers who take the Gospels as reliable history generally see two events; many others see one tradition told twice. Both groups can agree that Mark presents the feedings as signs that Jesus feeds both Israel and the nations.

hard.q: Did Jesus really predict his own death and resurrection, and could a crucified man be the Messiah?
hard.a:
The objection comes from two directions. Critical scholars since William Wrede (1901) and Rudolf Bultmann (1921) have argued that the detailed predictions in Mark (8:31; 9:31; 10:33-34) are prophecies composed after the event: they match the passion narrative too closely, they use the church's vocabulary, and the disciples' total incomprehension afterward seems hard to square with such plain speech. On this view the historical Jesus may have feared death, but the words ‘after three days rise again’ belong to the church's preaching. Jewish readers raise a deeper question. No text before Jesus clearly expects a Messiah who would be rejected by Israel's leaders and executed by Rome; the Messiah was to defeat Israel's enemies, rebuild the temple, and gather the exiles, and Jesus did none of these. A crucified Messiah is, in the Jewish objection, a contradiction the church invented to explain a failure, and Deuteronomy 21:23 declares a hanged man cursed.

Responses take the objections in turn. Many historians grant that the wording of the predictions has been shaped by the church's memory, while arguing that their core goes back to Jesus. Hans Bayer (1986) argued for a pre-Markan, Palestinian origin of the predictions of vindication, and N. T. Wright (1996) argued that Jesus, having acted against the temple and knowing John the Baptist's fate, could hardly have failed to expect death, and that he interpreted it from Israel's Scriptures (Isaiah 53; Daniel 7; the psalms of the suffering righteous) as the climax of Israel's story. The disciples' incomprehension, on this view, is historically plausible precisely because a dying Messiah contradicted everything they hoped. On the Jewish objection, Christian scholars concede that no pre-Christian text clearly joins the Messiah and the suffering servant, and they argue that Jesus himself joined them; Paul answers Deuteronomy 21:23 by saying Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Jewish interpreters, from Origen's opponent to Rashi to modern writers, have answered that the servant is Israel and that the Messiah's work remains unfinished. The church confesses that Jesus is the Christ because God raised him from the dead; the question of whether that confession is true is finally the question of the resurrection, which Mark's chapter points toward but does not yet narrate.

observe: Count the questions Jesus asks his disciples in verses 17 to 21. What does he want them to remember, and why?
In verses 30 to 33 the word rebuke appears three times. Who rebukes whom, and about what?
To whom does Jesus address the call in verse 34, and what three things does it require?
interpret: Why might Mark place the two-stage healing of the blind man right before Peter's confession? What does it suggest about Peter's sight?
Why does Jesus call Peter Satan, when Peter's words seem to come from love and loyalty?
What does it mean to lose one's life for Jesus' sake and the gospel's and so save it, and how does the double sense of psychē help?
apply: Peter got the title right and the meaning wrong. What do you expect of Jesus that might need to be corrected by the cross?
The blind man saw partly before he saw clearly. Where in your understanding of God do you still see people like trees walking?
What would it look like, concretely, for you to lose your life for Jesus' sake this week, and what are you afraid of losing?
